You are acting as the senior backend engineer responsible for auditing the existing Corvanta backend.

IMPORTANT:

* DO NOT modify any files.
* DO NOT refactor anything.
* DO NOT install packages.
* DO NOT create new files.
* DO NOT "fix" anything.
* This is an INFORMATION-GATHERING task only.
* Inspect the actual repository/source code rather than guessing from filenames.
* Be extremely detailed.
* Your report will be given to another senior developer who will use it to design and build the Corvanta React + TypeScript frontend.

I need a complete technical explanation of the CURRENT Corvanta backend.

## 1. PROJECT OVERVIEW

Explain in detail:

* What Corvanta is designed to do based on the actual implementation.
* The problem the backend solves.
* The major business capabilities currently implemented.
* The major modules/features.
* The architecture and how the major parts communicate.
* The technology stack.
* Runtime and Node.js version if determinable.
* Database technology.
* External services.
* AWS services currently supported or implemented.
* Development vs production behavior.
* Any important architectural decisions you find.

Do not invent product functionality that does not exist.

Clearly distinguish:

* implemented functionality
* partially implemented functionality
* infrastructure-ready functionality
* planned/intended functionality that is only implied by the code

## 2. COMPLETE DIRECTORY STRUCTURE

Provide a detailed directory/file tree of the backend.

For important files, explain:

* what the file does
* why it exists
* what other files depend on it

Pay particular attention to:

* entry point
* routes
* controllers
* services
* models
* middleware
* configuration
* validation
* utilities
* providers
* queues
* AWS integrations
* database layer
* authentication
* authorization
* error handling
* tests

## 3. ENTRY POINT

Give me the COMPLETE CURRENT CONTENT of the main application entry point, especially:

* index.js
* server.js
* app.js
* or whichever file actually starts the application

If index.js exists, provide its complete current content.

Do not summarize this section. I specifically need the actual source code.

Explain the entry point afterwards.

## 4. API INVENTORY

This is extremely important.

Find EVERY API endpoint currently implemented.

Create a detailed table containing:

* HTTP method
* complete route/path
* purpose
* controller
* service used
* authentication required?
* authorization/role requirements?
* request parameters
* query parameters
* request body
* validation rules
* successful response
* error responses
* relevant database models
* external services involved

Include ALL endpoints, not just major ones.

Group them logically by feature.

Example:

AUTH
POST /api/auth/register
POST /api/auth/login
...

Do not invent endpoints.

## 5. REQUEST AND RESPONSE SCHEMAS

For every important endpoint, document the actual request and response shape.

For example:

REQUEST:
{
...
}

RESPONSE:
{
...
}

Include:

* required fields
* optional fields
* data types
* enums
* nested objects
* IDs
* timestamps
* pagination structures
* error structures

This information will later be converted into TypeScript types/interfaces.

## 6. DATABASE

Explain the complete database architecture.

Identify every model/schema/table/document structure.

For each model explain:

* model name
* fields
* data types
* required/optional fields
* defaults
* enums
* indexes
* unique constraints
* relationships
* references
* validation
* timestamps
* important business rules

Explain how the models relate to one another.

If MongoDB/Mongoose is used, explain the schemas and relationships exactly as implemented.

## 7. AUTHENTICATION

Document the complete authentication implementation.

Explain:

* registration
* login

* password handling
* password hashing
* JWT/session handling
* token creation
* token validation
* refresh tokens if any
* cookies vs Authorization headers
* expiration

* protected routes
* current-user endpoint if any
* password reset
* email verification
* OTP
* account activation
* account approval

Only document functionality that actually exists.

## 8. AUTHORIZATION

Explain how the backend determines what a user is allowed to do.

Document:

* roles
* permissions
* middleware
* protected resources
* admin functionality
* ownership checks
* subscription/access checks

Show examples of protected endpoints.

## 9. VALIDATION

Document ALL important validation.

Identify:

* validation libraries
* schemas

* field limits

* authorization validation

Explain where validation occurs.

## 10. ERROR HANDLING

Explain the complete error architecture.

Include:

* custom error classes

* error response format
* validation errors

* external-service failures

Show the actual standard error response structure.

## 11. EXTERNAL SERVICES

Identify every external integration.

For each one explain:

## 12. QUEUE / ASYNCHRONOUS ARCHITECTURE

The backend contains an abstraction around queue providers.

Explain this architecture in detail.

Identify:

* queue interface
* InMemory provider
* SQS provider
* producers
* consumers/workers
* jobs/messages
* message payloads
* retry behavior
* failure handling
* environment switching
* how AWS SQS fits into production

Explain exactly how the application currently behaves.

## 13. AWS INTEGRATION

Document everything in the application that relates to AWS.

Include:

* S3
* SQS
* IAM assumptions
* credentials
* environment variables
* SDK packages
* queues
* buckets
* object operations
* production/development differences

Do not confuse application-level AWS code with Terraform infrastructure.

Clearly separate what the backend code implements from what Terraform provisions.

## 14. ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES

Find every environment variable referenced by the source code.

Create a table:

VARIABLE | PURPOSE | REQUIRED? | USED WHERE | EXAMPLE FORMAT

Do NOT expose real secrets.

## 22. FRONTEND CONTRACT

This is especially important.

Based ONLY on the actual backend implementation, tell the future frontend developer:

* what pages/features the frontend can currently support
* what authentication flows it needs
* what forms are required
* what data needs to be displayed
* what dashboards are possible
* what user actions are possible
* what API calls will be needed

Separate CURRENT backend capabilities from future product ideas.

## 23. BACKEND GAPS

Identify anything the frontend developer needs to know because the backend does NOT currently support it.

For example:

* frontend feature desired but no endpoint exists
* endpoint exists but lacks necessary data
* payment workflow incomplete
* subscription management incomplete
* user profile endpoint missing
* pagination missing
* etc.

Do not modify the backend.

## 25. COMPLETE FRONTEND HANDOFF

Finish with a section called:

"CORVANTA FRONTEND HANDOFF"

Give the future frontend developer a concise but complete technical briefing containing everything they need before touching the React project.

The briefing should include:

1. What Corvanta currently does
2. Backend architecture
3. API surface

5. database entities
6. important business rules
7. external services
8. AWS integration

FINAL REQUIREMENT:

At the end, provide a short "FACT CHECK" section with:

* confirmed from source code
* inferred from architecture
* not currently implemented
* unclear and requires clarification

Again:

DO NOT MODIFY THE REPOSITORY.

This is a forensic technical audit and frontend handoff document only.
